consensus_summary: The responses agree that west has no single settled symbolism, but repeatedly associate it with the setting or terminal side—ending, completion, decline, darkness, or death. They also recognize Hebrew yam (“sea/west”), east–west separation or totality, and occasionally westward movement toward a destination or divine presence.
book_summary: The book identifies west as the rearward endpoint or destination of a course. It grounds this in Israel’s east-facing compass, the western yam (“sea”) as the “hinder sea,” a related back/after/end/last word-family, and the east–west span of complete separation.
consensus_core_identification: West is the terminal or setting side, commonly signifying an ending, with east and west also marking maximal separation.
book_core_identification: West is the rearward endpoint—the place where a course ends or arrives—also associated linguistically with what is behind, last, or latter.
boundary_disagreement: The book retains the consensus category of terminality but defines it spatially and linguistically as rear, endpoint, destination, last, or latter. It does not foreground the consensus’s sunset-derived decline, darkness, death, or evil cases, while adding broader back/end word-family applications not ordinarily classified as symbolism of west.
material_contradiction: There is no direct contradiction at the minimum core: both identify west with an endpoint or ending. The material difference is that the book reclassifies terminality as an orientational and lexical relation rather than principally as sunset, decline, or death.
rationale: The book’s core is recognizable within the consensus: ending is prominent, yam as sea/west is explicitly listed, Psalm 103:12 supplies east–west separation, and one response even emphasizes westward destination. Nevertheless, the book materially redraws the category by centering rearward endpoint and related last/latter language while leaving aside many darker sunset associations. This is refinement rather than novelty or replacement.
strongest_objection: The cited texts clearly support the western sea as the hinder or utmost sea and east–west separation, but they do not by themselves establish that every related occurrence of behind, after, last, or latter symbolizes west, nor that west generally means “destination.” That broader lexical-symbolic synthesis requires linguistic argument beyond the printed excerpts.
